text.p: These are some of the leading stories in the Greek Cypriot press on Wednesday. Reuters has not verified these reports and does not vouch for their accuracy.
ALITHIA

- The government will not tolerate further arbitrary acts in Cyprus Airways, and if there is no move to rectify matters in the airline the government will not offer any financial support to the company, Finance Minister Christodoulos Christodoulou warns.
- A family of Cypriots in Athens refused to bury their dead child for 15 days, keeping him at home thinking he was in a coma.
- One man has been detained on suspicion of involvement in a bomb explosion in Nicosia last week.
CYPRUS MAIL
- Tourism warning. President Glafcos Clerides says irresponsible acts must not be allowed to harm the industry.
- The British army is willing to end its excercises at the environmentally-sensitive Akamas peninsula as soon as the government provides an alternative training site.
FINANCIAL MIRROR
- Brokerage houses disagree over calculations of the price earnings ratio on the Cyprus bourse.
- The Bank of Cyprus forecasts that its profits in 1998 will be up.
HARAVGHI
- Communist Akel party chief Demetris Christofias urges Britain to stop using the Akamas as an army training site.
- The Cyprus Ports Authority takes another step towards privatisation. There are no provisions for development projects in its 1997 budget.
PHILELEPHTHEROS
- All political parties are looking to a second round of presidential elections in February, as consultations among the opposition to field a common candidate have been inconclusive.
- A Filipina maid who gave birth to a little girl, abandoned her but was then found out is willing to give the child up for adoption in return for a job.
- Twelve priceless paintings have vanished from the walls of Limassol town hall. They disappeared three years ago but it was reported to police just yesterday.
SIMERINI
- The European Union and the United States have set their sights on achieving progress on the Cyprus problem and improving their relations with Turkey over the next six months.

- Eleni Foka, a Greek Cypriot teacher forced to come to the south to seek medical treatment, says she wants to return to the north and has asked the president to safeguard her freedom of movement there.
